meta.title: Amharic A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Amharic → English (see the Amharic, recall the meaning) and English → Amharic (see an English meaning, recall the Amharic). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Amharic, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 262 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, people and the family, numbers, time and the days of the week, food and drink, money and shopping, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, animals, school and work, the everyday verbs, and the pronouns, question words and joining words every sentence is built out of — and the other 238 are the commonest remaining words of the Amharic Wikipedia, counted by the WHOLE word: Amharic writes its prepositions and endings onto the word (ቤት 'house', ቤቱ 'the house', በቤቱ 'in the house'), so those forms are added together. That corpus is encyclopaedic, which shows in the fill (history, government, religion), and verbs are counted less well than nouns, so they rank lower than they are used. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here, and some of the commonest are missing from it (አዎ 'yes', እና 'and', ግን 'but', ለምን 'why', ሄደ 'to go'). Every word is in the Ethiopic script (fidäl), as Amharic is written; the Fidäl deck, first in this collection, teaches the letters. Beneath it is Wiktionary's romanisation, which also marks the doubled consonants the script leaves unwritten. A verb is shown by its dictionary form, the past 'he did' (ገዛ 'he bought', taught as 'to buy'), with its infinitive where Wiktionary gives one; a few verbs Wiktionary has only as an infinitive are taught by that (መምጣት 'to come'). A noun shows its gender, plural and definite form where Wiktionary has them. Several Amharic letters are said alike (ሀ ሐ ኀ, ሰ ሠ, አ ዐ, ጸ ፀ), so many words have two or three spellings; the card heads with the one the Amharic Wikipedia uses most and names the others. Example sentences are few: 93 of the 500 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about 250 Amharic sentences with a translation; none is invented. There is no speaker button: few devices have an Amharic voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Amharic Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

The Joint Development Authority of East African Countries (IGAD) and an institution that monitors the climate in the region issued a warning yesterday, indicating that there will be much less rain than expected, which could worsen the terrible drought.
